# Concept library

Use this when the first idea is too literal.

Do not copy a concept because it sounds clever. Pick the mechanism that expresses the message.

## Transformation concepts

### One object, many states

One object travels through the whole film.

Examples:
- note to plan to stage to screen to post
- seed to system to result
- card to room to dashboard
- dot to route to network

Good for:
- process
- end-to-end service
- product journey
- event production

### Build and reveal

The finished object assembles from its hidden parts.

Good for:
- craftsmanship
- operations
- identity
- systems

### Deconstruct to explain

Start with the clean result, then pull it apart into layers.

Good for:
- behind-the-scenes
- complexity
- quality
- technical work

### Compress and expand

A dense object becomes a simple one, or the reverse.

Good for:
- simplification
- scale
- summarization
- many-to-one relationships

## Spatial concepts

### Corridor of proof

Evidence passes through perspective and one proof item comes forward at a time.

Good for:
- portfolio
- milestones
- event history
- case studies

Use few proof items. Depth should imply abundance.

### Camera dives into detail

Begin with context, push into one meaningful detail, then reveal the larger consequence.

Good for:
- tiny error versus big audience
- one metric inside a business
- one component inside a system

### Foreground handoff

An object crosses the lens and becomes the next scene.

Good for:
- tactile collage
- fast social work
- event objects
- paper systems

### Negative-space reveal

The absence between objects forms the next symbol or word.

Good for:
- brand films
- identity work
- logo stories

## Light concepts

### Light as narrator

A spotlight, scanner, window, or beam reveals only what matters.

Good for:
- events
- stage
- luxury
- proof
- mystery

### Light becomes time

A rotating beam becomes a clock, dial, or progress sweep.

Good for:
- precision
- schedules
- countdown
- operations

## Path concepts

### One line through everything

A line travels through scenes and changes function.

It can be:
- route
- cable
- timeline
- underline
- chart
- map
- logo primitive

Good for:
- continuity
- process
- journeys
- systems

### Branch and converge

One source branches to channels, teams, countries, or outputs, then returns to one result.

Good for:
- distribution
- ecosystem
- omnichannel
- portfolio

## Typography concepts

### Type is the environment

Words are large enough to become walls, floors, masks, or paths.

Good for:
- manifestos
- teasers
- cultural work
- brand statements

### Type becomes layout

A word breaks into columns, rules, cards, or image frames.

Good for:
- editorial work
- content systems
- design stories

### Question and answer

A quiet question creates space. The answer arrives with a different scale or material.

Good for:
- hooks
- myths
- provocations
- CTA

### Word as physical object

A word can be stamped, folded, cut, printed, projected, lit, or assembled.

Good for:
- tactile styles
- branded campaigns
- event promos

## Time concepts

### Before, during, after

Show preparation, the live moment, and the value that remains.

Good for:
- events
- launches
- campaigns
- experiences

### One day compressed

Use time marks, changing light, schedules, and recurring elements.

Good for:
- operations
- logistics
- production

### Freeze the important instant

Everything stops except one signal.

Good for:
- proof
- risk
- insight
- turning point

## Data concepts

### Data becomes material

Bars become buildings.
Dots become audience.
A line becomes a route.
A network becomes a constellation.

Good for:
- business stories
- scale
- reach
- systems

Keep the underlying values truthful.

### One metric escapes the dashboard

The important number physically leaves a dense interface and takes over the frame.

Good for:
- KPI focus
- reports
- case studies

## Collage concepts

### Desk of evidence

The frame behaves like a working desk where papers, passes, plans, photos, and notes accumulate with purpose.

Good for:
- research
- history
- events
- documentary stories

### Poster wall

Posters or cards appear as a physical wall or stack, then one becomes the next scene.

Good for:
- campaigns
- event series
- cultural institutions

### Archive becomes present

Old material assembles into a current brand or event.

Good for:
- anniversaries
- heritage
- institutional stories

## Brand concepts

### Primitive as protagonist

One logo shape travels through the film and becomes different things.

Good for:
- identity
- brand systems
- launch films

### Brand color as event

The accent stays restrained, then fills the frame once at the most important brand beat.

Good for:
- strong brand recall
- palette discipline

### Logo assembled from callbacks

Objects or fragments from earlier scenes return and resolve into the mark.

Good for:
- endings
- full-circle stories

## Event-specific concepts

### What audience sees versus what team manages

Front-stage beauty splits into backstage plans, cue sheets, protocols, and timing.

Good for:
- event agencies
- conference production
- operations

### Guest journey

A pass, route, gate, seat, stage, and exit become one continuous path.

Good for:
- hospitality
- protocol
- event experience

### After the lights go out

The venue disappears but clips, quotes, media, photos, and recap assets continue outward.

Good for:
- content value after an event
- media coverage
- recap storytelling

## Product concepts

### Input becomes outcome

A real input travels through a system and returns as visible output.

Good for:
- software
- AI products
- tools

Use the real UI when possible.

### Feature as spatial transformation

A small card becomes a workspace, map, canvas, or system.

Good for:
- feature launches
- interface storytelling

## Choosing a concept

Score each candidate from 1 to 5 on:

- message fit
- visual clarity
- brand fit
- transition potential
- originality
- asset feasibility
- phone readability

Do not add the scores mechanically and call the highest one correct.

Use the scores to expose trade-offs, then choose the route whose mechanism best carries the message.
